newsitem.title: GREECE: GNN INTERVIEW: U.S. ENVOY SAYS CYPRUS CRISIS OVER, FOR NOW.
newsitem.headline: GNN INTERVIEW: U.S. ENVOY SAYS CYPRUS CRISIS OVER, FOR NOW.

text.p: U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh says the Cyprus missile crisis was over and tensions in the Eastern Mediterranean had been brought under control for the time being.
In an interview with Reuters Television, he said that he had assurances from Greek Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides that no missile parts would arrive on the island for more than a year.

"The assurances, and they were very solid assurances by President Clerides, that not a single component of this missile system would be brought to the island in the next 16 months made clear that in terms of a crisis (it) was defused," he said.
Cavanaugh said in the absence of even missile parts, there could be no reason for Turkey to carry out threats to launch a military strike.
Cyprus sparked the crisis this month by announcing it was buying Russian S-300 missiles, which would compromise Turkish air superiority in the volatile region.
Cavanaugh hoped the 16-month breathing space would be used to find a solution to the Cyprus problem and to dissuade Cyprus from going through with its plans to buy missiles.

"My hope is the missiles never come. It's my expectation, in fact, that the missiles will be unlikely ever to be deployed in Cyprus. The best way to solve that is to work towards a solution ... of the Cyprus problem," he said.
Cavanaugh was dispatched to defuse the missile crisis. He is meeting the leaders of the rival Greek and Turkish communities on Cyprus and their respective allies in Athens and Ankara.
He met Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash on Monday and Greek foreign ministry general secretary Alexandros Filon in Athens on Tuesday. He flies to Turkey on Wednesday.
Cavanaugh said tensions had soared recently. Greece and Turkey nearly went to war a year ago over disputed Aegean islets and clashes on Cyprus this summer left five people dead.

The United States, the European Union and the United Nations are trying to breathe new life into efforts to settle the Cyprus problem, which has poisoned relations between NATO allies Greece and Turkey for 23 years.
Washington has said Cyprus's purchase of the missiles was wrong and a setback for peace efforts but it has also said Turkish threats to strike at the missiles was unacceptable.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a coup attempt, inspired by a then-ruling military junta in Athens. Turkey has kept about 30,000 troops on the northern third of the island and a U.N. "green line" separates Greek and Turkish Cypriots.
Cavanaugh stood by statements that Denktash and Clerides both supported U.N. measures to reduce tension.
"A positive aspect of my visit in Cyprus...was agreement both by Mr Denktash and President Clerides to give their full support to the immediate implementation of those measures," he said.
"We hope to see that, in fact, starting to take place in the next few weeks," he added.

The U.N. measures are: 1) soldiers will not to use deadly force unless lives are threatened 2) arms will be unloaded in frontier areas so soldiers must load before firing 3) sentry posts will be unmanned.
Cavanaugh said these measures would promote the right atmosphere for face-to-face talks between Denktash and Clerides.

When told Cyprus had denied acceptance of the U.N. measures, he said both Denktash and Clerides "emphasised in no uncertain terms that they were prepared to provide their full support for the immediate implementation of the U.N. package of proposals".
"Hopefully both parties remain as fully committed as they were yesterday," he added. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
